name: Bumchu at Tashiding
when: Feb–Mar, 14th–15th day of the first Tibetan month (lunar calendar)
summary: Once a year the monks of Tashiding open a sealed vase of sacred water and measure it. The level is read as a forecast for Sikkim's coming year, and pilgrims queue through the night for a few drops.
body: Bumchu means 'sacred vase'. The vase at Tashiding Monastery is kept sealed all year and opened only on the night of the 14th and the morning of the 15th day of the first month of the Tibetan calendar, which falls in February or March. Monks measure the water in front of the crowd. The traditional reading is simple: a full vase promises a good year, a low level warns of scarcity, and cloudy or dirty water warns of trouble.

After the reading, the water is mixed and given to pilgrims as a blessing, and the vase is topped up with river water and sealed again for the next year. Pilgrims come from across Sikkim and from Nepal and Bhutan, and many stay up through the night in the monastery courtyard, among butter lamps, chanting and the smell of juniper smoke.

Tashiding itself is worth the trip at any time: a hilltop monastery founded in 1641 between the Rathong Chu and the Rangeet, with the Thongwa Rangdol chorten and long walls of carved mani stones. During Bumchu it is crowded and spiritual rather than a show for visitors, so come as a guest, not a spectator.
tips: Book a room in Tashiding, Yuksom or Pelling weeks ahead, because pilgrims fill every bed nearby
Carry a torch, a flask and warm layers if you plan to stay up through the night
Ask before photographing monks or the vase ceremony, and keep flash off

faqs.q: When is Bumchu held at Tashiding?
faqs.a: Bumchu follows the Tibetan lunar calendar: the 14th and 15th days of the first month, which usually falls in February or March. The exact dates move every year, so check the Sikkim government holiday list or ask the monastery or a local hotel. Check current status before you travel, as timings can shift.

Yes. Bumchu is a public religious festival and visitors are welcome if they behave as guests: dress modestly, keep to the edges of the crowd, do not push into the queue for blessed water unless you wish to receive it, and ask before taking photographs. Expect large crowds, little space and long waits.

faqs.q: What does the water level in the Bumchu vase mean?
faqs.a: By tradition the monks read the level as a forecast for the year ahead. A full vase is taken to mean peace and plenty, a low level points to drought or scarcity, and turbid water to unrest. The reading is announced publicly and discussed across Sikkim in the days after the festival.

faqs.q: How do I reach Tashiding for Bumchu?
faqs.a: Tashiding is about 19 km from Yuksom and about 40 km from Pelling. Shared jeeps run from Gyalshing and Jorethang, with extra vehicles at festival time, though seats go quickly. Many visitors stay in Yuksom or Pelling and come by reserved car. Leave early, because the last stretch of road jams up.

name: Pemayangtse Cham (masked dances)
when: Feb–Mar, the last days of the 12th Tibetan month, before Losar (lunar calendar)
summary: Two days of masked dances in the courtyard of Pemayangtse, Sikkim's leading Nyingma monastery, just before Losar. Monks in brocade and painted masks dance the defeat of evil, and the year's obstacles are symbolically destroyed.
body: Pemayangtse, 'the perfect sublime lotus', was founded around 1705 by the line of Lhatsun Chempo, one of the three lamas who crowned the first Chogyal at Yuksom in 1642. Its annual cham is held in the last days of the twelfth month of the Tibetan calendar, just before Losar, the Tibetan New Year, so it usually falls in February or early March.

Cham is a ritual, not a performance. Monks wearing masks of protector deities, skeleton dancers and animal-headed figures dance in slow, exact steps to long horns, cymbals and drums. The dances end with an effigy representing the year's evil being cut up and cast out, clearing the way for the new year. Families come from the villages around Pelling and Gyalshing dressed in their best.

The monastery courtyard is small and fills early, so arrive in the morning and expect to stand. Pelling is cold at this time, often 2–10 °C, but February and March also bring some of the clearest Kanchenjunga mornings of the year, so the festival pairs well with a quiet off-season stay.
tips: Arrive by 9 am to find a place on the courtyard steps
Dress warmly and modestly; Pelling mornings in February are close to freezing
Ask the monastery or your hotel for the exact dates, which follow the lunar calendar

faqs.a: The cham is held on the 28th and 29th days of the 12th Tibetan month, just before Losar, which puts it in February or early March. The Gregorian dates change every year. Ask the monastery or a Pelling hotel a few weeks ahead and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for the Pemayangtse cham?
faqs.a: The monastery charges a small entry fee to visitors on normal days, and festival arrangements can differ. Carry small notes for the entry and for offerings. The dances are religious ceremonies, so keep to the areas where local visitors stand and ask before photographing.

faqs.q: Where should I stay for the Pemayangtse cham?
faqs.a: Stay in Upper Pelling, about 2 km and 30 minutes on foot from the monastery. February is low season, so rooms are cheaper than in October or April, and many budget hotels discount. Ask for a room with a heater or extra blankets, as nights drop close to freezing.

faqs.q: Can I combine the cham with Losar and Bumchu?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Losar starts the day after the cham ends, and Bumchu at Tashiding falls on the 14th–15th of the first month, about two weeks later. A two-week stay between Pelling, Yuksom and Tashiding can take in all three, if the calendar suits. Check current status before you travel.

name: Pang Lhabsol at Ravangla
when: Aug–Sep, 15th day of the 7th Tibetan month (lunar calendar)
summary: A festival unique to Sikkim that honours Mount Kanchenjunga as the guardian deity of the land. Warrior dances, a masked figure of the mountain god on a snow lion, and a memory of the blood brotherhood between Lepchas and Bhutias.
body: Pang Lhabsol means roughly 'the worship of the witness gods'. It honours Dzonga, the spirit of Mount Kanchenjunga, as Sikkim's guardian deity, and it recalls the oath of brotherhood sworn in the 13th century between the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and the Bhutia chief Khye Bumsa, with the mountain called on as witness. It is a festival of Sikkim alone, celebrated by Buddhists across the state.

The centre of the day is the pangtoed cham, a warrior dance by men in helmets and armour carrying swords and shields, together with a masked figure representing Kanchenjunga riding a snow lion. Ravangla holds one of the largest celebrations, often with a multi-day cultural programme in the town alongside the monastery rituals; Gangtok's Tsuklakhang has the other famous one.

The festival falls in late August or September, at the tail of the monsoon. Expect rain, mist and leeches on forest paths, but also green hills, few tourists and low room prices. Roads in South Sikkim can be hit by landslides at this time of year, so leave a buffer day.
tips: Keep a buffer day in your plan: late monsoon landslides can delay jeeps
Ask in Ravangla which day the warrior dances are held, as programmes vary
Carry an umbrella and a rain jacket rather than relying on the morning sky

faqs.a: Pang Lhabsol is a Sikkimese Buddhist festival honouring Mount Kanchenjunga as the guardian deity of Sikkim. It also commemorates the blood brotherhood between the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and the Bhutia chief Khye Bumsa, sworn with the mountain as witness. Its best-known element is a warrior dance by armoured dancers alongside masked deities.

On the 15th day of the 7th month of the Tibetan calendar, which falls in late August or September. It is a Sikkim state holiday, so the date appears in the state's annual holiday list. Ravangla often adds a cultural programme around it; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Ravangla a good place to see Pang Lhabsol?
faqs.a: Yes. Ravangla holds one of the biggest Pang Lhabsol celebrations in Sikkim, and the town is small enough that you can walk between the venues. Rooms are cheaper than in peak season, but the festival draws visitors from across the state, so book a few days ahead.

faqs.q: What is the weather like during Pang Lhabsol?
faqs.a: It is the end of the monsoon. Expect daily rain or drizzle, mist that comes and goes, and temperatures around 13–20 °C in Ravangla. Views of Kanchenjunga are rare at this time. Pack a rain jacket, quick-drying shoes and salt or spray for leeches if you walk in the forest.

name: Tendong Lho Rum Faat
summary: The Lepcha festival of Tendong Hill, held every 8 August, giving thanks to the hill that, in Lepcha tradition, rose above a great flood and saved their ancestors. Prayers, songs and dances across Sikkim, with special meaning around Namchi.
body: Tendong Hill rises above Namchi and Damthang to about 2,600 m. Lepcha tradition tells of a great flood, when the rivers Rangeet and Teesta rose and the water covered the land. The Lepcha people climbed Tendong and prayed, and the hill rose higher like a horn, keeping them above the water until it fell. Tendong Lho Rum Faat, roughly 'the prayer to the god of Tendong Hill', is the thanksgiving for that rescue.

Today it is held on 8 August and is a state holiday in Sikkim. Lepcha associations hold prayers led by bongthings (Lepcha priests), with traditional songs, dances, archery and food. Some groups also climb towards the hill itself. For visitors it is a rare chance to see Lepcha dress, music and language in public, and to understand that the Lepchas, Sikkim's earliest known people, see this landscape as sacred.

August is monsoon season, so expect rain and possible road delays. Namchi is about an hour from Ravangla and makes a good base; Damthang, the starting point for the Tendong walk, lies between the two.
tips: Ask a Lepcha association or your hosts where public celebrations are held that year
Do not attempt the Tendong climb in heavy rain; the trail is slippery and leech-prone
Dress modestly and ask before photographing prayers led by bongthings

faqs.q: What is Tendong Lho Rum Faat?
faqs.a: It is the Lepcha festival honouring Tendong Hill, near Namchi. In Lepcha tradition, the hill rose up during a great flood and saved the Lepcha people who took refuge on it. The festival gives thanks for that rescue with prayers led by Lepcha priests, songs, dances and community meals.

faqs.q: When is Tendong Lho Rum Faat celebrated?
faqs.a: On 8 August every year, a fixed date that is a public holiday in Sikkim. Unlike most Buddhist festivals here it does not move with the lunar calendar. Events are organised by Lepcha associations, so locations change from year to year. Check current status before you travel.

Yes. The usual walk starts near Damthang, between Namchi and Ravangla, and climbs through forest to the top at about 2,600 m in roughly 3 to 4 hours. In August the trail is wet and leech-prone, so most visitors save the climb for October to April and attend the festival in town.

faqs.q: Where can I learn more about Lepcha culture in South Sikkim?
faqs.a: Ask your homestay hosts, many of whom are Lepcha or have Lepcha neighbours, and visit during Tendong Lho Rum Faat if you can. In West Sikkim, Rinchenpong and Kaluk have Lepcha heritage displays. For a deeper visit, Dzongu in North Sikkim is the Lepcha reserve, though it needs a separate permit.
